turns.q: Which parts of the layout make the “Continue Shopping” and “Place Order” bars feel like they have equal weight instead of one clearly standing out?
turns.a: I suppose it was the coloring. Everything on the page was in roughly the same... palette, I want to say. Nothing really contrasted with anything else. So my eye didn't go anywhere in particular. I'm not sure if that's intentional — maybe they wanted a calm, quiet look — but it made it harder to find the action.

turns.q: What would the “Place Order” bar need to look like for it to stand out clearly as the main action on this screen?
turns.a: I think because buttons need to tell you they're buttons. When you look at a screen, you're scanning for the thing you're supposed to do, and usually the most prominent thing is that thing. If the button is the same shade as the background, it stops looking like a button and starts looking like a label or a decorative element. You stop registering it as actionable.

turns.q: If you were fixing this, what specifically would you change about the “Place Order” bar so it looks like a real button instead of a label or decorative element?
turns.a: I think most people — most of the time — don't read everything on a screen. They scan for signals. Color contrast, size, position — those are the signals that say 'this is what you interact with.' If those signals aren't there, you have to work harder. And for a primary action — the one thing the screen exists to do — making someone work harder to find it feels like it's working against the purpose of the page.

turns.q: What would make the “Place Order” bar clearly recognizable as the primary action when you first look at this layout?
turns.a: I think I've said most of what I have to say about it. I keep coming back to the same point because that's where the concern actually is — it's not something more complex underneath. At least not from where I'm standing. It's genuinely just about visibility.

turns.q: What specific visual change would make the “Place Order” bar visible enough to read as the main action at first glance?
turns.a: Because the whole point of that screen is to get someone to place an order. If the primary action that does that is nearly invisible — and I mean that somewhat literally, it was very pale text on a pale background, small font — then the screen is failing at its one job. It's not just friction. It's a broken affordance. You've designed an action that people can't see to take. The fix is direct: give the 'Place Order' button a solid fill color that contrasts with the background — not gray on gray — and make the text large enough to read at a glance. Something that immediately reads as 'this is what you press.' That's it. That's the root of it and the fix for it.
